title: A Saturday at the market
paragraphs: Every Saturday, Efua goes to the big market in the city centre. She usually leaves home at seven o'clock, before the streets get busy. She takes a shared taxi because it is cheaper than a private one.

At the market, she buys vegetables, fish and rice for the whole week. She always visits the same seller, Mrs Agbo, because her tomatoes are fresh and her prices are fair. They often chat about their families.

This Saturday is different. Efua is not shopping for food. She is looking for a present for her brother, who is graduating next week. After an hour, she finds a beautiful leather bag. It is expensive, but she decides to buy it. "He will use it every day at his new job," she thinks.

shared.def: used by several people at the same time

chat.def: to talk in a friendly, informal way

summary: Efua shops at the market every Saturday, always from the same seller. This week she buys a leather bag as a graduation present for her brother.

title: How mobile money changed daily life
paragraphs: Twenty years ago, sending money to a relative in another town was slow and risky. People often gave cash to a bus driver or travelled for hours to deliver it themselves. Today, in many West African countries, a few taps on a basic phone are enough.

Mobile money services allow users to store money in an account linked to their phone number. They can transfer it, pay bills or buy airtime without a bank account. This has been especially important for people in rural areas, where banks are rare and often far away.

Researchers have found that families who use mobile money are better able to deal with emergencies, such as an illness or a poor harvest, because relatives can send help quickly. Small traders also benefit: they can receive payments from customers they have never met.

However, the system is not perfect. Transaction fees can be high for small amounts, and fraud — for example, fake messages asking users to send money back — remains a problem. Experts argue that better digital education is as important as new technology.

emergencies.def: sudden dangerous situations needing quick action

harvest.def: the crops collected in a season

traders.def: people who buy and sell goods

summary: Mobile money lets people transfer and store money with a phone, which helps rural families, emergencies and small traders. Problems remain: high fees for small amounts and fraud, so digital education is needed.

title: Why sleep helps you learn
paragraphs: Many students believe that staying up late is the best way to prepare for an exam. Scientific studies suggest the opposite: sleep plays an essential role in learning.

During the day, the brain collects new information. At night, especially during deep sleep, it reorganises this information and transfers important memories to long-term storage. In one well-known type of experiment, people who slept after learning a list of words remembered more of them the next day than people who stayed awake.
Sleep also affects attention. After a short night, it is harder to concentrate, and we make more mistakes. This is why a tired student may read the same page several times without understanding it.
For language learners, the message is clear: regular short study sessions followed by a good night's sleep are more effective than one long session the night before a test.

storage.def: a place where things are kept

summary: Sleep helps learning because the brain reorganises and stores memories at night and attention is better after rest. Short regular sessions plus sleep beat one long late-night session.

title: Brain drain or brain gain?
paragraphs: Every year, thousands of young Africans leave their countries to study or work abroad. Doctors move to the United Kingdom, engineers to Canada, and students to France, Germany or China. For decades, this movement was described as a 'brain drain': the departure of talented people whose education had been paid for by their home countries, which then lost their skills.

The costs are real. In some countries, more doctors trained locally now work abroad than at home, and hospitals struggle to replace them. Governments argue that they invest heavily in universities only to see graduates contribute to the economies of richer nations. Critics add that recruitment campaigns by foreign health services make the problem worse.

However, a growing number of economists question this pessimistic view. They point out that migrants send home remittances worth more than all international aid combined, money which pays for school fees, small businesses and medical care. Moreover, the possibility of working abroad encourages more young people to pursue higher education in the first place, and not all of them actually leave.

There is also the phenomenon of 'brain circulation'. Many professionals return after several years, bringing new skills, international networks and capital. Others remain abroad but invest in start-ups, mentor students online or create partnerships between universities. In this sense, the diaspora can become a bridge rather than a loss.

Whether migration is a drain or a gain therefore depends largely on policy. Countries that offer attractive conditions for returnees, recognise foreign qualifications and involve their diaspora in development projects tend to benefit most. The question, experts conclude, is not how to stop people from leaving, but how to make sure that their success abroad also benefits those who stay.

drain.def: a continuous loss of something valuable

recruitment.def: the process of finding new people to work for an organisation

remittances.def: money sent by migrants to their families at home

pursue.def: to try to achieve something over time

returnees.def: people who come back to their country after living abroad

diaspora.def: people from one country who live in other countries

mentor.def: to advise and help a less experienced person

capital.def: money used to start or develop a business

summary: Skilled migration costs African countries talent, but remittances, returnees and diaspora networks can turn it into a gain, depending on government policy.

title: Kofi's day
paragraphs: Kofi is 24. He is from Kpalimé, but he lives in Lomé with his sister Ama. Kofi is a mechanic and Ama is a nurse.
Kofi gets up at six o'clock. He has breakfast — bread and tea — and goes to work by moto. His garage is next to a big market.
Ama works at night, so she sleeps in the morning. On Sundays, Kofi and Ama visit their parents in Kpalimé. They love their mother's food!

garage.def: a place where cars are repaired

title: Will AI tutors replace teachers?
paragraphs: Few technologies have entered classrooms as rapidly as generative AI. Within two years of its public release, students on every continent were using chatbots to summarise readings, check grammar and, inevitably, write essays. Predictably, the debate has polarised: enthusiasts herald a revolution in personalised learning, while sceptics warn of a generation that outsources thinking itself.

The case for AI tutoring rests largely on a well-established finding. Decades of research indicate that one-to-one tutoring dramatically improves outcomes compared with conventional classroom instruction. Until now, such tutoring has been prohibitively expensive; an AI that adapts to each learner at negligible cost could, in principle, democratise it.

Yet the evidence so far is more nuanced than either camp suggests. Several studies have found that students who rely on AI to solve problems perform well during practice but worse on subsequent tests, arguably because the tool removes the productive struggle through which durable learning occurs. Where AI was configured to give hints rather than answers, however, the decline largely disappeared.

What emerges, then, is less a story of replacement than of redesign. Teachers remain indispensable for what machines do poorly: motivating reluctant learners, reading a room, and modelling intellectual curiosity. The more pressing question is not whether AI belongs in education, but how institutions can harness it without eroding the very skills education is meant to build.

herald.def: to announce something as important and coming

outsources.def: gives work to an outside person or system

prohibitively.def: so much that people cannot afford it

negligible.def: so small it is not important

harness.def: to control and use something for a purpose

summary: AI tutoring could make one-to-one help cheap, but it harms learning when it gives answers; the future lies in redesigning teaching, not replacing teachers.
